messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elena Weber is a 78-year-old graphic designer who has worked from a home studio for years, taking on logo and layout projects for local businesses. She traces the beginning of her difficulties to a hurricane that struck her coastal town three years ago. She and her husband stayed through the storm, believing their house would hold. During the night, the wind changed direction and the back door began slamming against its frame hard enough to shake the walls. Water pushed under the threshold, the power failed, and in the dark she could hear neighboring houses breaking apart. At one point, when they were later taken to a temporary shelter, the sharp smell of spilled rubbing alcohol and liquor from broken containers mixed with wet wood and mildew; she remembers hearing strangers speak in hushed, stunned voices about people who had not been found and families who had lost someone. Those details have remained painfully alive for her.

In the months after, Elena found that ordinary moments could abruptly pull her back into the disaster. If a delivery person let the front door bang shut, or if she heard a heavy door open in the hallway of her apartment building, she would feel a jolt of alarm and think immediately that safety is always temporary, that the world can turn catastrophic without warning. News stories or even casual conversation about someone losing a spouse or child could leave her preoccupied for hours with the conviction that no life is protected from arbitrary devastation. Passing someone who smelled of alcohol in the grocery store or elevator could do the same. Each of these moments seemed to confirm what she had come to believe since the hurricane: the world is dangerous, the basic rules she once trusted have been shattered, and what happened to her and her neighbors was profoundly unfair.

Those beliefs have not stayed abstract. Elena has become consumed with the idea that the catastrophe should somehow have been prevented. She goes over weather reports, evacuation notices, and decisions made by local officials, dwelling on what might have been done differently and what she and her husband should have done sooner. Around the house she repeatedly cleans, straightens, and reorganizes shelves, counters, and her design desk until everything looks controlled and exact. She describes trying to keep disorder from “getting a foothold.” She also works hard to push the hurricane out of her mind altogether, cutting off images as soon as they arise and telling herself not to think about it. These habits make sense to her because she is certain that if the world is this unsafe and unjust, she must stay vigilant and keep things under control wherever she can.

Her beliefs also shape the way she remembers the storm. When she speaks about that night, there are moments when the memory does not feel like a memory at all but as if she is back in the blacked-out house hearing the door slam again. At other times she recounts the scene in a flat, distant way, almost puzzled by her own lack of feeling, saying it is like hearing about something that happened to another woman. She often says the whole event feels unreal, too extreme to fit with the life she thought she had. The more she sees the world as permanently dangerous and morally broken, the less the hurricane feels like something completed and placed in the past.

That unstable quality of memory has fed her efforts to manage it. When the scene comes back with a here-and-now force, she starts wiping kitchen surfaces, rearranging drawers, or scrubbing the bathroom grout until her body settles. When the recollection goes numb and unreal, she becomes even more determined to blot it out entirely, as though refusing it might stop it from returning in a more vivid form. Yet over time these strategies seem to have kept the memory both raw and unprocessed. The more forcefully she tries to erase it, the stranger and less fully integrated it feels; the more she relies on cleaning and mental review to contain it, the easier it is for a slamming door or the smell of alcohol to set off the same old surge. Even in her work as a designer, she now keeps her studio door propped open so she will not hear it latch, and she avoids meeting certain clients in person if she thinks she might have to pass through busy office corridors with heavy doors.

By the time Elena sought help, her life had narrowed around these precautions. Her husband had begun commenting that the apartment looked “like a showroom nobody can live in,” and she had turned down collaborative projects because she no longer wanted to work in other people’s spaces. What finally brought her in was a recent episode when a neighboring apartment door slammed and, for several seconds, she was certain she was back in the storm. Afterward she spent the rest of the day cleaning in silence and that night lay awake thinking again about everything that had not been prevented. She says she is frightened that this is how the rest of her life will be: one sound, one smell, one conversation away from disaster. What she wants most is to feel that the hurricane is over, and that the world, while imperfect, is not about to break open every time a door moves.
